title: Senior's toolkit: modern LINQ operators
summary: The .NET 6 to .NET 10 operators that replace hand-written loops and clumsy GroupBy chains, and how to measure a pipeline.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: modern LINQ operators
steps.body: Recent .NET versions added operators for the jobs people used to write by hand: counting by key, totalling by key, batching, indexing, left joins. Knowing them makes queries shorter, faster and easier to review.

toolkit.what: Count items per key in one pass, without building groups (.NET 9). Returns `KeyValuePair<TKey, int>` items.
flags: the old way: keeps every item of every group in memory
toolkit.example:
foreach (var (status, n) in tickets.CountBy(t => t.Status))
    Console.WriteLine($"{status}: {n}");

toolkit.what: Fold items into one running value per key, such as a total per customer, in one pass (.NET 9).
flags: the starting value for each key, e.g. `0m`
toolkit.example: var revenue = orders.AggregateBy(o => o.CustomerId, 0m, (sum, o) => sum + o.Total);

toolkit.what: Get each item with its position as an `(Index, Item)` tuple (.NET 9), instead of a separate counter or `Select((x, i) => ...)`.
toolkit.example:
foreach (var (i, line) in File.ReadLines(path).Index())
    if (line.Length > 200) Console.WriteLine($"line {i + 1} is too long");

toolkit.what: Split a sequence into arrays of at most N items. The usual way to send rows to a database or an API in batches.
flags: the batch size; the last batch can be smaller
toolkit.example:
foreach (var batch in ids.Chunk(500))
    await api.DeleteManyAsync(batch, ct);

toolkit.what: A left outer join in one call (new in .NET 10): every outer item, with the match or `null`. Before .NET 10 it took `GroupJoin` + `SelectMany` + `DefaultIfEmpty`, which you will still see in older code.
toolkit.example:
var rows = customers.LeftJoin(orders, c => c.Id, o => o.CustomerId,
    (c, o) => new { c.Name, Total = o?.Total ?? 0m });

toolkit.what: Set operations by a key (.NET 6): "customers with no order", "users in both lists", without writing a comparer.
flags: items whose key is not in `keys`
both lists, first one wins per key
toolkit.example: var neverOrdered = customers.ExceptBy(orders.Select(o => o.CustomerId), c => c.Id);

toolkit.what: When a LINQ pipeline is on a hot path, compare it with a loop in a benchmark before rewriting it. Read Mean (time per call) and Allocated (bytes per call) together.
flags: adds the Allocated and Gen0 columns

steps.prompt: A nightly job runs `events.GroupBy(e => e.Country).Select(g => new { g.Key, Count = g.Count() })` over 50 million events and its memory climbs to 12 GB before it is killed. What is the smallest change that fixes it?
options: `events.CountBy(e => e.Country)`: it keeps only one counter per country instead of every event of every group
Run the job on a machine with 32 GB
steps.explain: `GroupBy` has to buffer every element of every group before the first group is yielded. `CountBy` streams and stores one integer per key, so memory depends on the number of countries, not on the number of events.
`CountBy` yields keys in the order they were first seen. Seven items in chunks of three give three chunks (3, 3, 1). `Index()` numbers from 0.

steps.prompt: Match each operator to the job.
pairs: line numbers while reading a file
every customer, with their order or null

steps.prompt: Total revenue per customer in one pass.
steps.code: var revenue = orders.__1__(o => o.CustomerId, __2__, (sum, o) => sum + o.Total);
steps.explain: `AggregateBy` takes a key, a seed for each key and a fold function. `Aggregate` produces a single value for the whole sequence, not one per key. The seed is `0m` because `Total` is a `decimal`.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When you see `GroupBy` followed by `Count()` or `Sum()`, reach for `CountBy` or `AggregateBy`. Batch external calls with `Chunk`. On hot paths, compare the query with a loop in BenchmarkDotNet and choose with the numbers, not by taste.
